name: Investment grade bond laddering
heading: The Structural Opportunity: Earning the Credit Spread
caseLead: The investment case rests on the credit spread, the extra yield that investment grade companies pay over government bonds for the risk of default and for lower liquidity. The spread persists because investors price in rare but severe credit losses, and because geopolitical and policy shocks regularly raise the cost of corporate borrowing even though most investment grade issuers repay in full.
caseRest: The main risk is a sharp widening in credit spreads together with higher government bond yields, which lowers bond prices faster than coupon income can replace the loss. A ladder reduces reinvestment risk, but it does not protect the market value of the bonds before they mature. In 2022 and in March 2020 the portfolio lost value even though almost all of the bonds were later repaid at par.
figNote: The large figure on each card shows the widest level of the investment grade credit spread during the episode. The spread is the extra yield that US investment grade corporate bonds pay over Treasuries, which has averaged about 1.5% over the long run, and readings above 3% signal severe stress.

events.title: Bank failures push credit spreads above 6%
events.text: After the Lehman Brothers failure, the investment grade spread reached 6.1% in December 2008 as banks and other financial issuers lost market access. The strategy lost because bond prices fell sharply and refinancing risk rose, although most bonds were repaid at maturity.

events.title: ECB corporate bond buying narrows spreads
events.text: The investment grade spread peaked near 2.2% in February 2016 during the oil price slump, then narrowed after the European Central Bank announced corporate bond purchases in March. The strategy gained because the staggered maturities kept income steady and bond prices recovered.

events.title: Fed backstop ends the Covid credit sell-off
events.text: The investment grade spread rose to 4.0% in March 2020, and it narrowed after the Federal Reserve announced corporate bond purchases on 23 March. Results were mixed because bond prices fell sharply and then recovered, while maturing bonds were repaid at par.

events.title: Fed rate rises cause a record bond loss
events.text: The Federal Reserve raised rates by 75 basis points at four meetings in 2022, and the investment grade spread reached 1.7% in October. The strategy lost because higher Treasury yields lowered bond prices much more than wider spreads did.

events.title: Bank failures widen spreads only briefly
events.text: The failure of Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023 pushed the investment grade spread to about 1.6% as investors questioned bank funding. The strategy gained because the widening was brief and maturing bonds were reinvested at higher yields.

events.title: US tariffs lift credit spreads for weeks
events.text: The US tariff announcement of April 2025 widened the investment grade spread to about 1.2% as investors expected weaker earnings. Results were mixed because bond prices fell for a few weeks, while the ladder's short maturities limited the loss.

instrument: US and European investment grade corporate bonds rated BBB- or higher; maturities of 1 to 7 years; one rung matures each year
rules: Issuers selected with net debt below 3.5 times earnings; no issuer above 3%; bonds sold on a downgrade to BBB- with a negative outlook; maturing bonds reinvested at the longest rung
costs: Estimated bid-ask spreads on purchases and sales; no trading costs on bonds held to maturity

Provides collateral and earns the cash rate

entry: Bond spread at least 0.8% over Treasuries of the same maturity
size: No issuer above 3% and no sector above 20%
exit: Held to maturity, or sold on a downgrade to BBB- with a negative outlook
stop: Longest rung halved if the investment grade spread closes above 2.5%
marketWatch: Rehyn monitors the investment grade spread over Treasuries, the share of bonds rated BBB and the level of corporate leverage, because these show how much compensation investors receive for credit risk. Central bank rate decisions, new issuance volumes and tariff announcements that affect earnings are the events that matter most. A widening in spreads would reduce portfolio value, while a fall in Treasury yields would raise it.

favourable.heading: Stable credit spreads
favourable.text: Stable spreads favour the strategy because bonds earn their coupon without price losses and maturing bonds are reinvested at current yields. Between 2012 and 2019 the investment grade spread mostly stayed between 1% and 2%, so income made up most of the return.

favourable.heading: Higher yields on reinvestment
favourable.text: Higher yields favour the strategy over time because each maturing rung is reinvested at the new rate, which raises the income of the whole ladder. After the 2022 rate rises, the yield on investment grade bonds reached about 6% in late 2023, more than double the level of 2021.

favourable.heading: Central bank support for credit
favourable.text: Central bank support favours the strategy because purchases and lending facilities lower credit spreads and keep issuers able to refinance. In March 2020 the Federal Reserve announced corporate bond purchases, and the investment grade spread fell from 4.0% to below 2% by June.

adverse.heading: Rising rates and inflation
adverse.text: Higher yields hurt the strategy because bond prices fall when rates rise and the ladder keeps its bonds until they mature. In 2022 the 10-year Treasury yield rose about 235 basis points, and Rehyn estimates that the ladder lost about 14% from peak to trough.

adverse.heading: A sharp widening in spreads
adverse.text: Wider spreads hurt the strategy because falling prices reduce portfolio value even though most bonds are repaid at par. In March 2020 the spread rose from about 1% to 4% in five weeks, and issuers of weaker investment grade bonds lost access to the market.

adverse.heading: Downgrades to high yield
adverse.text: Downgrades hurt the strategy because bonds that fall below investment grade are sold by funds that must hold higher-rated debt, which pushes prices down. In 2020 about 200 billion dollars of bonds were cut to high yield, including bonds issued by Ford.

infoHist: Historical results show the strategy's peak-to-trough drawdown during each event, measured from the ladder's value just before the event to its lowest point using the default backtest parameters above. Each event window runs from the last high in bond prices before the shock to the low.
infoForward: Scenario results show the estimated profit or loss over the first month of each scenario. Rehyn's scenario engine projects moves in Treasury yields and investment grade spreads, which are then applied to the ladder's current maturities and issuers.
